<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with tight, vivid framing. A's best work was the "unwitnessed / unaware victim" line and the clever attempt to convert B's "enforcement manufactured the counterfeit pill" claim into a concession that supply composition governs mortality; A also exposed a genuinely weak spot when B's answer to the unwitnessed death leaned on supervised consumption sites that barely exist in the U.S. But A's route to victory always depended on interdiction actually delivering fewer milligrams, and B kept that burden squarely alive: fentanyl has no harvest to fail, chokepoint wins have historically been re-routings, and A's own concession that "the remaining question is only direction" left the causal claim asserted rather than demonstrated. B's asymmetry reframe answered A's symmetry counter cleanly — enforcement was tested at maximum force with rising deaths, while medication treatment was never scaled enough to be tested — and B's closing killed A's single cleanest natural experiment by distinguishing a crop-based heroin drought from a lab-regenerated synthetic. B also landed the decisive comparative: A's "superior reach" is conditional on a border holding against a molecule, a condition never once achieved, whereas MAT's mortality effect is measured per person reached. A's unanswered geographic-timing point (eastern states declining first) and last-word rebuttal of B5.4 keep this competitive, and A's clipped opening is a small execution cost. On net B left the stronger unneutralized burden on the table.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing dismantling of A's Australia heroin-drought example — conceding it was a real supply disruption but showing it depended on a crop and season that fentanyl does not have — removed A's only historical instance of supply disruption bending a mortality curve, while B's "one tool failed at maximum, the other was never scaled" reframe defused A's symmetry counter.</best_rebuttal>
